title: Hash tables: hashing, collisions and collision handling
learningObjectives: Explain the topic and its C rules.
Trace the example and explain its data or control flow.
Identify edge cases and resource-management requirements.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: A hash table maps keys to bucket positions using a hash function. Collisions occur when distinct keys map to the same bucket. Separate chaining stores multiple entries per bucket; open addressing searches for another available slot according to a probe sequence.
understand.whyItMatters: A hash function alone is not a complete hash table. Correctness requires collision resolution, key equality, capacity management and resizing rules.
understand.analogy: Treat each algorithm or resource as a contract whose invariants must remain true after every operation.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for pointers, object lifetime, complexity or library contracts.

explain.narrative:
A hash table maps keys to bucket positions using a hash function. Collisions occur when distinct keys map to the same bucket. Separate chaining stores multiple entries per bucket; open addressing searches for another available slot according to a probe sequence.

State preconditions, invariants, empty and full cases, ownership and failure behaviour before implementation. Compile with warnings and test normal, boundary and failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The function chooses a bucket index for nonzero capacity. A complete table must still compare keys and handle multiple keys that map to the same bucket.

practise.guidedTask: Give two distinct keys that map to the same bucket for a small capacity.
practise.independentTask: Implement separate chaining for integer keys and test collisions, deletion and resizing.
hints: A hash match does not mean the original keys are equal.
Keep equality consistent with the key representation.
Rehash entries when the bucket array capacity changes.
